What are Hands-off Flow conditions?

'Hands-off Flow' (HoF) conditions come into effect when the flow rate drops below a certain level. When this happens most abstractors are issued an alert (although some abstractors self-monitor) and abstraction is limited or stopped until the flow rate increases.

HoF conditions are measured in megalitres per day. One megalitre is equivalent to 1000 cubic metres. For reference, an Olympic sized swimming pool is 2.5 megalitres in size.

Your licence may have a different HoF condition applied depending on your use and exact abstraction point location.

What are Hands-off Flow bands?

Hands-off Flow (HoF) conditions are grouped into bands and this gives you an idea of how water stressed your local water body is.

Band 1 has the most water available and fewest restrictions, while band 6 is the most water stressed with no water available left for licensing.

Once the remaining water in the band has been licensed, the water body will move into the next band up and the restrictions will increase.

What is a common end date?

The 'common end date' indicates when the licensing strategy for this area is due for review. The Environment Agency review each local licensing strategy every 12 years.

Most licences expire on the common end date but sometimes a shorter time limit is needed, usually due to local issues or uncertainty. If you want to abstract water after the expiry date, you must apply for a new a licence to replace the existing one.

You can apply for a longer licence period of up to 24 years which is granted at the discretion of the Environment Agency.

If the next common end date is over 6 years away, it will usually apply to your licence as the expiry date. If it is less than 6 years away, in most cases we will skip to the next common end date and apply that to your licence instead.

Local policies affecting water availability in {{data.riverCatchmentData[data.sid].properties.WB_NAME}}

The Environment Agency has local policies which may affect water availability in your area. These policies are designed to protect the environment and ensure that water is used sustainably.

{% if data.sid == "1" %}
Local policy Details
Heavily Modified Water Body (HMWB)
What is a Heavily Modified Water Body?
Some water bodies are designated as 'artificial or heavily modified because they have been created or modified to suit a particular purpose such as water supply, flood protection or navigation. They are often known as regulated rivers and may be managed through an operating agreement held by a water company which determines the availability of water.

Within the South and West Somerset wider catchment area there are several water bodies that are designated as HMWB, including the LDE areas, rivers affected by reservoirs and reservoirs themselves. There are also several lakes and drain water bodies which are designated artificial. These systems provide flows to support 'protected areas' within these catchments.

Throughout both the Brue and Parrett catchments, many of the water bodies are heavily modified due to the artificial nature of the landscape.

If the water body is a HMWB then this may impact on the availability of water. A local assessment is required for any applications for new water to determine whether there is resource available. Conditions including HoF or HoL restrictions may be applied to your licence.
Level Dependent Environment (LDE)
What is a Level Dependent Environment?
A Level Dependent Environment (LDE) is an area where water levels are influenced by the surrounding topography and drainage systems. These environments are characterised by a network of river channels flowing above the level of the surrounding land. The low-lying land has a network of drainage ditches. These ditches remove water from the low-lying land and in many cases are pumped into the main river channels during the winter or high flows.

The South and West Somerset catchment contains a significant area of level dependent environments (LDEs). Flow constraints may not apply in LDEs. Local constraints based on levels not flow may be required on a site-specific basis to protect the watercourses.

The Somerset Levels and Moors of the Brue, Parrett and Tone catchments are a managed wetland system covering an area of approximately 650km2. Most of the water in the Moors lies in a network of manmade channels (known locally as 'rhynes'). These rhynes serve several roles:

  1. irrigating the Moors (for wet fences and supplying drinking water for livestock)
  2. draining the areas after periods of high rainfall
  3. flooding in certain areas for conservation purposes

The water levels are artificially controlled by structures including pumping stations, gates and sluices.
Internal Drainage Board (IDB)
What is an Internal Drainage Board?
An Internal Drainage Board (IDB) is a public body that manages water levels in an area, known as an internal drainage district, where there is a special need for drainage. We will consult the relevant IDB for any licence that is considered in an IDB area.

The Internal Drainage Boards have an important role in managing the water levels in the rhynes within the low-lying levels and moors. The Environment Agency controls larger pumping stations and tidal gates.

Water level management plans have been set up for the LDEs. These have been agreed by the bodies or authorities interested in the water level management in an area. The Somerset Drainage Board Consortium maintain most of these plans, although the Environment Agency also operate a number.

Local policy Details
Heavily Modified Water Body (HMWB)
What is a Heavily Modified Water Body?
Some water bodies are designated as 'artificial or heavily modified because they have been created or modified to suit a particular purpose such as water supply, flood protection or navigation. They are often known as regulated rivers and may be managed through an operating agreement held by a water company which determines the availability of water.

Water availability in this area is determined on a case-by-case basis because of the HMWBs. A local assessment will be required for any new applications before granting a licence. This affects licence applications as local assessments cost extra and can take time to organise and process.

A Hands-off Level restriction may be applied to your licence instead of/as well as a Hands-off Flow restriction. A Hands-off Level is used where the water is measured by how high or deep the water level is in your area, rather than by how fast it is flowing. This restriction may reduce the number of days you can take water across the year.
Level Dependent Environment (LDE)
What is a Level Dependent Environment?
A Level Dependent Environment (LDE) is an area where water levels are influenced by the surrounding topography and drainage systems. These environments are characterised by a network of river channels flowing above the level of the surrounding land. The low-lying land has a network of drainage ditches. These ditches remove water from the low-lying land and in many cases are pumped into the main river channels during the winter or high flows.

Your local LDE is The Somerset Levels and Moors.

Most of the water in this local area lies in a network of manmade channels (known locally as 'rhynes'). These channels serve a specific purpose and so abstraction licences are limited to the following uses:

  • nature conservation
  • creating water meadows
  • wet fencing
  • animal watering welfare

Abstraction licences for these uses are only available for the winter period in this area (1 November to 31 March). Licences will not be granted for the summer months.
Internal Drainage Board (IDB)
What is an Internal Drainage Board?
An Internal Drainage Board (IDB) is a public body that manages water levels in an area, known as an internal drainage district, where there is a special need for drainage. We will consult the relevant IDB for any licence that is considered in an IDB area.

Your local IDB is The Somerset Drainage Board Consortium.

Water level management plans have been set up for the LDEs and these determine water licence availability. The Somerset Drainage Board Consortium maintain most of these plans, although the Environment Agency also operate a number.

We recommend you consult the Somerset Drainage Board Consortium before applying for a licence to see how this could affect you.
